newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel's Netanyahu battles scandal report.
newsitem.headline: Israel's Netanyahu battles scandal report.

text.p: Israel's embattled leader Benjamin Netanyahu faced fresh criticism on Tuesday as police were completing investigations which a newspaper said could lead to charging him with corruption.

"I am sure and convinced the prime minister's hands are clean," Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh said of a Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper report police were struggling over whether to recommend charging Netanyahu with fraud and breach of trust.

Police are looking into the appointment last January of an attorney general. Israel's Channel One Television has alleged a Netanyahu ally on trial pushed candidate Roni Bar-On for the job in hopes of winning a plea bargain.
A police spokeswoman said investigators would probably submit recommendations on Tuesday to the state prosecutor who would decide whether to bring charges against anyone in the government.
The man on trial, Aryeh Deri of the religious Shas party, denies any wrongdoing. Bar-On himself quit hours after being appointed amid criticism he was professionally unfit for the job.

The scandal has cast a giant shadow over Netanyahu's government at a time peace moves are deadlocked over his start of a Jewish settlement and an explosion at a Tel Aviv cafe that killed three Israeli women and the Palestinian bomber.

Netanyahu has also been battling charges by a leading industrialist of being a poor manager and a report he has been speaking with one voice to Israelis and another to an outside world critical of his Jewish settlement policy.

Benny Gaon, chief executive officer of Koor Industries Ltd, Israel's largest holding company, last week assailed Netanyahu for a "failing management" and accused the prime minister of ignoring Israel's business community.

"I told Netanyahu I am ready to be your bridge to the business community. Consult us, come to us, speak with us. It was like sending a fax without an answering system...Bibi doesn't answer," Gaon told Yedioth Ahronoth on Friday.

On Monday, Yedioth Ahronoth said Netanyahu, under world pressure over his Jewish settlement policy, had promised Italy's prime minister to delay for three years the controversial building of houses for Jews on a hill in East Jerusalem.
When Netanyahu broke ground on the Har Homa Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on March 18, he said he was asserting a right of Jews to live anywhere in the holy city.
"We obviously won't agree to change our stance on this issue and we've made this unequivocally clear," Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak said on Monday in reaction to the report.

But much of the world has criticised Netanyahu, saying he should not try to pre-empt peace deals with Palestinians which leave to talks running until May 1999 the fate of East Jerusalem, an area claimed by both sides.

Netanyahu, locked in a coalition with right-wingers like himself who oppose peace deals requiring him to swap more land for peace with Palestinians, has in recent days said he might forge a government with the Labour party he ousted last May.
While opposing the peace deals has said he will honour Israel's international obligations.

But commentator Yoel Marcus, writing in the newspaper Haaretz on Tuesday, said Netanyahu should not be trying to save his political life by turning to the party which launched the peace deals with Palestinians he opposes.

"A prime minister who acknowledges the failure of his policies and believes he has lost his political base, doesn't forge deals based on the ideology of the opposition, but resigns and asks anew for the voters' trust," Marcus wrote.
